literal: The arrow struck Zhi in the eye, and he lost sight in that eye.
idiomatic: The shaft struck Zhi's eye, and he lost sight in it.

literal: An edict appointed Zhi to administer Hengzhou.
idiomatic: He was ordered to govern Hengzhou.

literal: In Emperor Xuanwu's time he was appointed regional inspector of Jingzhou; on returning to court, Censor-in-Chief Wang Xian memorialized that while in the province Zhi had coerced purchase of free persons as slave-girls and also overclaimed supplies.
idiomatic: Under Xuanwu he became inspector of Jingzhou; back at court, Censor Wang Xian charged that in the province he had forced free people into bondage as maidservants and skimmed supplies.

literal: He was pardoned when an amnesty was proclaimed.
idiomatic: An amnesty cleared him.

literal: At the start of Emperor Xiaozong's reign he concurrently served as Minister of Justice.
idiomatic: At Xiaozong's accession he also served as Minister of Justice.

literal: Later he was made regional inspector of Yangzhou and granted the barony of Jianzhong.
idiomatic: He was later made inspector of Yangzhou and enfeoffed Baron of Jianzhong.

literal: In the province his prestige, though less than Li Chong's, still made Jing and Chu fear him.
idiomatic: In office his name, though below Li Chong's, still awed Jing and Chu.

literal: Soon he was made regional inspector of Yongzhou.
idiomatic: He was soon transferred to Yongzhou.

literal: In his later years he indulged in music and performers; while in Yangzhou he kept nearly a hundred attendants at his side, with vessels and dress of rare splendor unsurpassed in the age.
idiomatic: In old age he doted on music and players; at Yangzhou nearly a hundred attendants stood by him, with gear and dress unrivaled in splendor.

literal: In Yongzhou he went further in luxury, amassing wealth without limit, and his reputation suffered.
idiomatic: At Yongzhou he grew still more extravagant, extorted without end, and his repute collapsed.

literal: When Moqi Niansheng rebelled, an edict made Zhi Western Campaign commander-in-chief to attack him.
idiomatic: When Moqi Niansheng rose, Zhi was ordered west as campaign commander to crush him.

literal: Niansheng sent his younger brother Tiansheng to garrison Longkou [17] and confront Zhi.
idiomatic: Niansheng sent his brother Tiansheng to hold Longkou [17] and face Zhi.

literal: Seized by the enemy's advantage, he abandoned the main force and fled back to Qizhou.
idiomatic: Outmaneuvered, he abandoned the main army and fled to Qizhou.

literal: The rebels then besieged the city.
idiomatic: The rebels then laid siege.

literal: Regional inspector Pei Fenzhi suspected the townspeople of secret collusion with the rebels and was about to drive them all out; Zhi would not consent.
idiomatic: Inspector Pei Fenzhi suspected the citizens of colluding with the enemy and meant to expel them all; Zhi refused.

literal: The townspeople indeed opened the gates and admitted the rebels; they chained Zhi and Fenzhi and sent them to Niansheng, who killed them.
idiomatic: The people opened the gates to the rebels, chained Zhi and Fenzhi, sent them to Niansheng, and they were killed.

literal: At the start of the Deposed Emperor's reign he was posthumously made Vice Director of the Masters of Writing and Grand Guardian.
idiomatic: Under the Deposed Emperor he was posthumously made Vice Director of the Masters of Writing and Grand Guardian.

literal: Duke Chuzhen of Fufeng was a descendant of Emperor Lie.
idiomatic: Chuzhen, Duke of Fufeng, was descended from Emperor Lie.

literal: In youth he was known for fierce valor.
idiomatic: As a youth he was famed for boldness.

literal: He reached Director of the Palace Secretariat, was granted the dukedom of Fufeng, was entrusted with great affairs of state, and was greatly honored.
idiomatic: He rose to Director of the Palace Secretariat, was made Duke of Fufeng, entrusted with major policy, and treated with high honor.

literal: The Tujing Hu led by Cao Puhun and others rebelled and called in the Shuofang Hu as allies.
idiomatic: The Tujing Hu under Cao Puhun rebelled and summoned Shuofang Hu allies.

literal: Chuzhen, with Prince Na of Gaoliang and others, attacked and destroyed them.
idiomatic: Chuzhen, with Prince Na of Gaoliang and others, crushed them.

literal: By nature greedy, in the army he was fierce and cruel; for an offense he was executed.
idiomatic: Greedy by nature and brutal in the field, he was executed for an offense.

literal: Duke Ni of Wen'an was a distant member of the imperial clan.
idiomatic: Ni, Duke of Wen'an, was a collateral of the house.

literal: By nature loyal, upright, and fierce, with strategic talent.
idiomatic: He was loyal, blunt, and bold, and skilled in planning.

literal: Emperor Daowu treated him generously, granted him the dukedom of Wen'an, and appointed him General Who Pacifies the East.
idiomatic: Daowu favored him, made him Duke of Wen'an, and appointed him General Who Pacifies the East.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He passed away.

literal: His son Qu inherited the title.
idiomatic: His son Qu succeeded.

literal: In Emperor Mingyuan's time he served at the Gate Department, issuing and receiving edicts.
idiomatic: Under Mingyuan he served at the Gate Department, handling edicts in and out.

literal: By nature clever and quick, skilled at memorializing, he always matched the sovereign's intent; he was granted the marquisate of Yuancheng, made General of Meritorious Service, and with Duke of Nanping Changgun Song, Marquis of Baima Cui Xuanbo, and others jointly decided lawsuits.
idiomatic: Clever and quick in memorials, he always hit the mark; he was made Marquis of Yuancheng and General of Meritorious Service, and with Changgun Song of Nanping, Cui Xuanbo of Baima, and others judged legal cases.

literal: When Mingyuan toured the east he ordered Qu to act as Right Chancellor and Marquis of Shanyang Xi Jin as Left Chancellor, entrusting them with army and state—his reputation was great.
idiomatic: On Mingyuan's eastern tour Qu served as Right Chancellor and Xi Jin of Shanyang as Left, in charge of army and state, and won great repute.

literal: Later the Tujing Hu and the Lishi Hu led by Chu Yibing and others rebelled [18], set up commanders, and called in Helian Qubing from outside.
idiomatic: Later the Tujing and Lishi Hu under Chu Yibing and others rebelled [18], appointed officers, and called in Helian Qubing.

literal: Qu directed Duke of Kuaiji Liu Ji and Marquis of Yong'an Wei Qin to resist; Qin perished in battle, Ji fell from his horse and was seized by the Hu and sent to Qubing—only Qu's force remained.
idiomatic: Qu led Liu Ji of Kuaiji and Wei Qin of Yong'an to resist; Qin died in the ranks, Ji fell and was taken to Qubing, and only Qu's troops were left.

literal: Mingyuan, because Qu had lost two generals, wished to execute him.
idiomatic: Mingyuan, angry that Qu had lost two generals, meant to kill him.

literal: At the time Bingzhou inspector Yuan Liutou was dissolute and negligent in office, so Qu was pardoned and ordered to act as provincial governor.
idiomatic: Bingzhou inspector Yuan Liutou was dissolute and slack, so Qu was spared and told to take over the province.

literal: Qu gave himself to drink and largely neglected government; Mingyuan, tallying his earlier and later faults, had him brought back in a caged cart and executed in the market.
idiomatic: Qu drank heavily and neglected rule; Mingyuan, weighing old and new faults, had him caged back to the capital and beheaded in the market.

literal: His son Mohun was known to Mingyuan from youth.
idiomatic: His son Mohun had been known to Mingyuan since boyhood.

literal: When Yuan Shao's rebellion came, Mingyuan hid outside the palace; Mohun and Shusun Jun falsely declared where Mingyuan was.
idiomatic: In Yuan Shao's revolt Mingyuan hid outside; Mohun and Shusun Jun feigned knowledge of his whereabouts.

literal: Shao sent two men from his tent to follow Mohun, intending treason.
idiomatic: Shao sent two tent guards after Mohun to plot treason.

literal: Once Mohun was out, he bound the tent guards and took them to Mingyuan, who executed them.
idiomatic: Mohun got out, bound the guards, brought them to Mingyuan, and they were killed.

literal: Mingyuan, gaining Mohun, was greatly pleased and took him as a close supporter.
idiomatic: Mingyuan rejoiced to have Mohun and made him a close ally.

literal: For merit he was granted the dukedom of Changsha, appointed Master of Writing, and sent out as regional inspector of Dingzhou.
idiomatic: For merit he was made Duke of Changsha and Master of Writing, then sent out as inspector of Dingzhou.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He passed away.

literal: Collation notes
idiomatic: Textual notes

literal: Wei shu juan 14: In the tables of contents of the various editions this juan is marked "deficient." The Baipu, Nan, Ji, and Ju editions all have Song-dynasty collation notes at the end of the juan stating: "The Wei shu biographies of the descendants of Emperors Shenyuan and Pingwen are lost; later persons supplemented them from the Beishi, and also added material from the Gaoshi xiaoshi.
idiomatic: Wei shu juan 14: Several editions mark this scroll deficient in their tables of contents. Baipu, Nan, Ji, and Ju copies carry a Song note at the juan's end: the Shenyuan and Pingwen descendants chapters of Wei Shou are missing; later editors patched them from Beishi and padded them with Gaoshi xiaoshi.

literal: Later juan in which Wei Shou's original history is lost all follow this practice.
idiomatic: Later volumes with lacunae in Wei Shou's original follow the same rule.

literal: The Dian edition's textual verification says: "Wei Shou's book is lost; later persons supplemented it."
idiomatic: The Dian edition's Kaozheng says: "Wei Shou's text is gone; what follows is later supplementation."

literal: Now separated by mountains. Cefu juan 271
idiomatic: Now the mountains lie between. Cefu juan 271

literal: 〈folio 3214〉
idiomatic: folio 3214

literal: Below "mountain" is the character "river."
idiomatic: The graph for "river" appears below "mountain."

literal: Comment: By the sense this character should be present.
idiomatic: Note: The sense requires that character.

literal: Then widely recruited empty carts going out from the capital. In all editions and Beishi juan 15 the character "recruit" is left blank; now supplemented according to Cefu juan 678
idiomatic: Then widely recruited empty carts leaving the capital. All editions and Beishi juan 15 leave the graph for "recruit" blank; it is supplied from Cefu juan 678

literal: 〈folio 8100〉
idiomatic: folio 8100

literal: Supplemented.
idiomatic: The reading is supplied.

literal: As to public business not being sent to the censor. Beishi juan 15 has the character "wei" before "send"; Tongzhi juan 80, Wei Imperial Clan biography, has the character "ming" after "send."
idiomatic: On whether public business should be sent to the censor: Beishi juan 15 has wei before "send"; Tongzhi juan 80 (Wei imperial clan) has ming after "send."

literal: Comment: "Wei send" does not fit the sense.
idiomatic: Note: "Wei send" will not parse.

literal: Below it says Yuan Shun "would not give the names," and again: "It is not fitting to subordinate them to the censor-in-chief; send the names to the censor."
idiomatic: Below, Yuan Shun "would not supply the names," and again: "They should not be subordinated to the censor-in-chief; the names should go to the censor."

literal: The dispute at the time concerned whether so-called "public business"—that is, assemblies of officials—should have name lists sent to the Censorate, not whether all public business of the Masters of Writing should go to the Censorate.
idiomatic: The fight was over whether "public business"—meetings of officials—required name lists to the Censorate, not whether every secretariat matter belonged there.

literal: Here the character "ming" is missing after "send."
idiomatic: Here ming is lost after "send."

literal: Again, searching the Wei shu biography of Cui Yan and the Jin Wenyang□ biography of Fu Jia, both say that once censor-in-chief the hundred officials trembled. Qian's Kaoyi juan 38 says: "Comment: In the Three Kingdoms biographies of Cui Yan and Fu Jia, neither says they served as censor-in-chief.
idiomatic: Again, Wei shu's Cui Yan and the Jin Wenyang□ life of Fu Jia both say that as censor-in-chief the hundred officials trembled. Qian Daxin, Kaoyi juan 38: "Note: Neither Three Kingdoms life makes them censor-in-chief.

literal: 'Jin Wenyang' may be suspected as a corruption for 'Jin Yangqiu.'
idiomatic: 'Jin Wenyang' may corrupt 'Jin Yangqiu.'

literal: Yet Jia was a Wei man, not a Jin man.
idiomatic: Yet Jia was a Wei subject, not a Jin one.

literal: Comment: This Wei shu should be Wang Shen's Wei shu.
idiomatic: Note: The Wei shu meant here is Wang Shen's book.

literal: "Jin Wenyang" may be a corruption for "Jin Yangqiu"; though Fu Jia was a Wei man, his ties to the Sima clan were deep, and his deeds may have been narrated there.
idiomatic: "Jin Wenyang" may stand for "Jin Yangqiu"; though Jia was Wei-born, his closeness to the Sima house may have put him in that work.

literal: Chang's younger brother Zhen, courtesy name Jinque, inherited the barony of Ailing. In all editions and Beishi juan 15 "que" is written erroneously as "sheng"; now emended according to the epitaph in Muzhi jishi, Yuan Zhen's epitaph
idiomatic: Chang's brother Zhen, styled Jinque, inherited the barony of Ailing. All editions and Beishi juan 15 write que as sheng; the reading follows Yuan Zhen's epitaph in Muzhi jishi

literal: 〈plate 44〉
idiomatic: plate 44

literal: Emended.
idiomatic: Corrected accordingly.

literal: The epitaph also calls Zhen "enfeoffed lord of Jinyang," and does not say he inherited the barony of Ailing.
idiomatic: The epitaph also calls Zhen enfeoffed at Jinyang, not heir to Ailing.

literal: According to the biography of Zhen's father Ping above, he inherited the marquisate of Songzi and was also granted the barony of Ailing for military merit.
idiomatic: Per the life of Zhen's father Ping above, he inherited Songzi and received Ailing for military merit.

literal: When Ping died, the eldest son Chang inherited the marquisate of Songzi; the barony of Ailing should have been inherited by Zhen—hence this biography's wording.
idiomatic: When Ping died, Chang took Songzi; Ailing should have passed to Zhen—hence the biography's wording.

literal: According to Chang's biography, at the Taihe demotion of ranks he was granted the barony of Ailing as earl—probably at that time Zhen was changed to Baron of Jinyang; hence the epitaph's "enfeoffed territory" and not "inherited title."
idiomatic: Chang's life says that at the Taihe demotion he received Ailing as earl—likely when Zhen was shifted to Jinyang baron, so the epitaph says "fief" rather than "inheritance."

literal: Biography and epitaph illuminate each other; the biography need not be wrong.
idiomatic: Life and epitaph complement each other; the biography need not be in error.

literal: Such cases in which enfeoffments, offices, names, and posthumous titles differ between history and epitaph are many; where history's error cannot be fixed, collation notes will not be given each time hereafter.
idiomatic: Rank, office, name, and posthumous title often diverge between history and epitaph; where the history cannot be proved wrong, notes will not be repeated for every case.

literal: Youzhou, former Beiping prefecture registrar, Xing Guo of Hejian. Zizhi tongjian juan 152
idiomatic: Youzhou, former registrar of Beiping prefecture, Xing Guo of Hejian. Zizhi tongjian juan 152

literal: 〈folio 4750〉
idiomatic: folio 4750

literal: "Beiping" is written "Pingbei."
idiomatic: Beiping appears as Pingbei.

literal: Comment: Beiping commandery in Wei belonged to Pingzhou, not Youzhou, and could not be called a "prefecture."
idiomatic: Note: Beiping commandery belonged to Pingzhou, not Youzhou, and could not be styled a prefecture.

literal: "Pingbei" was a military title borne at the time by a certain regional inspector of Youzhou; under Wei regulations, generals of fifth rank and above who opened an office had registrars.
idiomatic: "Pingbei" was the army title of a Youzhou inspector; under Wei rules, fifth-rank generals and above who opened offices had registrars.

literal: Here "Beiping" should be the inverted error for "Pingbei."
idiomatic: Here Beiping is a transposition for Pingbei.

literal: When the Secretariat reported culling and simplifying the granted commanderies and counties. In all editions and Beishi juan 15 this sentence reads "When the Secretariat reported rest and simplification in granting commanderies and counties."
idiomatic: When the secretariat reported culling the granted commanderies and counties: all editions and Beishi juan 15 read "When the secretariat reported rest and simplification in granting commanderies and counties."

literal: All editions also annotate "doubtful" below.
idiomatic: All editions also mark "doubtful" below.

literal: Tongzhi juan 80 quotes as above.
idiomatic: Tongzhi juan 80 has the passage as quoted above.

literal: Comment: "Rest and simplification in granting commanderies and counties" cannot be parsed; "culling and simplifying the granted commanderies and counties" refers to culling the refugee prefectures and counties set up for Hebei migrants, among which was Xin'an commandery, originally intended for Xing Guo as administrator.
idiomatic: Note: "Rest and simplification in granting commanderies" is nonsense; "culling the granted commanderies and counties" means trimming the refugee prefectures set up for Hebei migrants, including Xin'an, first slated for Guo.

literal: The uncleared Hejian commandery was then given to Guo's younger clansman Ziyao, hence "Guo was deeply shamed and resentful."
idiomatic: When Hejian was not cut, it went to Guo's cousin Ziyao, hence Guo's deep shame and resentment.

literal: Viewing the context before and after, Tongzhi is correct; emended accordingly.
idiomatic: The context shows Tongzhi is right; the text is emended accordingly.

literal: Held the offices Master of Writing, regional inspector of Yongzhou, and in sequence Vice Director of the Ministry of Revenue and regional inspector of Huazhou. Beishi juan 15 is the same.
idiomatic: Offices held: Master of Writing, inspector of Yongzhou, and in turn Vice Director of Revenue and inspector of Huazhou. Beishi juan 15 agrees.

literal: Comment: This biography is abbreviated; text is probably missing.
idiomatic: Note: The life is abbreviated; text is likely missing.

literal: Juan 6, Annals of Emperor Xianzu, Tian'an year 1, records "Director of the Palace Secretariat, Grand General Who Guards the West, Duke of Xihe Yuan Shi" rescuing Xuanchi.
idiomatic: Juan 6 (Xianzu) records that in Tian'an year 1 "Director of the Palace Secretariat, Grand General Who Guards the West, Duke of Xihe Yuan Shi" relieved Xuanchi.

literal: The affair also appears in juan 56, biography of Zheng Yi, and juan 61, biography of Chang Zhenqi—it should not be absent from Shi's own biography.
idiomatic: The same affair appears in juan 56 (Zheng Yi) and juan 61 (Chang Zhenqi) and ought not be missing from Shi's life.

literal: Moreover, as the annals write it, Shi's noble rank was "Duke of Xihe."
idiomatic: Moreover the annals give Shi the rank Duke of Xihe.

literal: This biography does not mention enfeoffment but only calls him "Minister over the Masses"—another sign of lacuna.
idiomatic: This life names no enfeoffment but only "Minister over the Masses"—another lacuna.

literal: Permanently receive exemption from corvée. In all editions "yong" is written "qiu."
idiomatic: "Permanently receive exemption from corvée": every edition writes yong (permanent) as qiu (seek).

literal: Comment: This was a special privilege granted by Yuan Hong to Yuan Pi, not something Pi requested; the character "qiu" will not parse.
idiomatic: Note: Yuan Hong granted Yuan Pi this privilege; he did not request it, and qiu will not parse.

literal: Juan 44, biography of Gou Ti, and juan 93, biography of Wang Rui, both have the phrase "permanently receive exemption from corvée," showing that here "qiu" is a corruption of "yong"; now corrected.
idiomatic: Juan 44 (Gou Ti) and juan 93 (Wang Rui) both have "permanently receive exemption from corvée," proving qiu corrupts yong; corrected here.

literal: Master of Writing Yu Guo said. In all editions "Guo" is written "Gao"; Zizhi tongjian juan 139
idiomatic: Master of Writing Yu Guo spoke: all editions write Guo as Gao; Zizhi tongjian juan 139

literal: 〈folio 4352〉
idiomatic: folio 4352

literal: has "Guo."
idiomatic: has Guo.

literal: Comment: Yu Guo is attached in this book juan 31 and Beishi juan 23, biography of Yu Lüpi.
idiomatic: Note: Yu Guo appears in this book juan 31 and Beishi juan 23 (Yu Lüpi).

literal: The Tongjian is correct; now emended accordingly.
idiomatic: Tongjian is right; the text follows it.

literal: The Central Plains are as this passage intends. This sentence cannot be parsed; there must be corruption and lacuna. Zizhi tongjian juan 139
idiomatic: "The Central Plains are as this intends": the line will not parse and must be corrupt or lacunose. Zizhi tongjian juan 139
